title: CFD Validation of the NASA ASJ ARN2 Nozzle in ANSYS Fluent
goal: Run and document a CFD validation study of compressible subsonic flow through the NASA ASJ ARN2 converging nozzle in ANSYS Fluent (SST k-omega turbulence model), compare the results against the NASA benchmark, and turn everything into a clear, well-formatted technical report with an introduction that is accessible to non-experts.
context: I am an aerospace and mechanical engineer, and this session is a CFD (Computational Fluid Dynamics) project. CFD uses a computer to simulate how a fluid moves by dividing the flow region into a mesh of small cells and numerically solving the governing equations in each cell. My task is to reproduce a well-documented NASA benchmark — subsonic, compressible air flow through the ARN2 converging nozzle (NASA's “Axisymmetric Subsonic Jet” case) — and to check that my simulation matches NASA's published data. Because a trustworthy result depends heavily on mesh quality and on the choice of turbulence model, the workflow runs from setting up and meshing the geometry in ANSYS, to running and troubleshooting the simulation, to analysing the jet, and finally to writing everything up as a clear report that a non-specialist could also follow. I chose this goal because it is a real, self-contained engineering task that combines simulation, analysis, and technical writing, and realistically takes more than an hour.
occupation: Aerospace & mechanical engineer (freelance CFD / CAD consultant)

session_goal_achievement.Why or why not: I completed a meshed, axisymmetric half-model simulation with the SST k–ω model and produced the full report. However, the exit Mach number came out at about 0.40 instead of the benchmark value of about 0.51; I traced this to a meshing problem (insufficient resolution near the nozzle) that I did not have time to fully re-mesh and re-run within the session. I had also planned to compare a second turbulence model (Spalart–Allmaras, SA) but ran out of time, so only SST k–ω was completed. The documentation part of the goal was fully achieved; the validation target was only partially achieved.

Step 1.step_name: Understand the ASJ ARN2 benchmark and plan the ANSYS setup / build the ARN2 nozzle geometry
Step 1.step_action: I asked Claude to explain the NASA Axisymmetric Subsonic Jet (ASJ) ARN2 case in plain terms - the nozzle geometry, the inlet/outlet boundary conditions, the target exit Mach number (~0.51), and the SST k-omega near wall requirement (y+ ~ 1) - and used its answer to plan my geometry, mesh strategy, and solver settings before opening ANSYS.

nodes.label: Review the NASA ARN2/SMC000 nozzle reference drawing and set up the ANSYS Workbench project
nodes.detail: The participant has a browser PDF of the NASA reference paper open showing dimensioned ARN2/SMC000 nozzle profiles (diameters 8.500/6.500/6.000 in, 30 degree angle), alongside idle Claude and Messages tabs. She opens ANSYS Workbench, drags in a Fluid Flow (Fluent) system, and opens Geometry in DesignModeler, explaining that of the four NASA reference nozzles (ARN1, ARN2, ARN3, SMC000) only ARN2 will be modeled, and only half of it, exploiting axisymmetry.

nodes.label: Build the nozzle profile point table in Excel from the reference polynomial
nodes.detail: In Excel she builds a point table for the nozzle profile curve using the polynomial equation from the reference drawing, y = 0.0125821*x^3 - 0.18881*x^2 + 3, evaluated for x = 0 to 6.825 in in increments of 0.2, generating 36 (x, y, z=0) points. She exports the resulting table as a text file for import into DesignModeler.

nodes.label: Construct the half-nozzle wall geometry in DesignModeler from the imported point curve
nodes.detail: Back in DesignModeler she sets units to inches, uses Concept > 3D Curve to import the exported point file as a curve, creates a new plane, and projects the imported line body onto it. She then sketches the remaining short profile segments (a horizontal/vertical line pair dimensioned 0.665 in and 0.250 in with a 30 degree angle from the axis) to close out the nozzle wall profile.

Step 2.step_name: Build the geometry and generate the mesh in ANSYS
Step 2.step_action: I built the 2D axisymmetric half-model in ANSYS DesignModeler and generated the mesh, using edge sizing and inflation to refine the shear layer and wall boundary layers. I produced 1 mesh - coarse (70,600 elements).

nodes.label: Finish building the 2D axisymmetric half-model surface geometry in DesignModeler
nodes.detail: The participant continues sketching the closing profile lines on Plane5 (dimensioning edges, setting angle constraints), then generates a Line-Body-to-Surface conversion (Surf1) from the closed line body, producing a '2 Parts, 2 Bodies' tree with a Line Body and a Surface Body representing the half-nozzle flow domain in inches.

nodes.label: Ask Claude for the criteria that define a good 2D mapped mesh in Fluent
nodes.detail: Before setting up mesh controls, she opens the Claude chat and asks 'what are the criteria for a good mapped mesh on ansys fluent for a 2d fluid domain'.

nodes.label: Apply edge sizing, bias, and quad-layer controls in ANSYS Meshing to build the coarse structured mesh
nodes.detail: Switching to ANSYS Meshing, she applies a series of Edge Sizing controls (Edge Sizing through Edge Sizing 17) with number-of-divisions and bias-factor settings (e.g. a bias factor of 1500 near the nozzle throat curve) to cluster cells toward the wall and shear layer, following the skewness/aspect-ratio/growth-rate criteria Claude just described. She adds sizing and quad-layer settings visible in the Mesh ribbon to keep the domain as a mapped quad mesh.

nodes.label: Check mesh quality metrics and launch the Fluent solver
nodes.detail: After generating the mesh she reviews the Mesh Metrics worksheet (orthogonal quality: min 0.150, average 0.895; aspect ratio average ~40.8, max ~7880) confirming an acceptable quad-dominant structured mesh of about 70,600 elements, then opens the Fluent Launcher and selects 2D, double precision, before starting Fluent.

nodes.label: Answer for the criteria that define a good 2D mapped mesh in Fluent
nodes.detail: Claude's visible reply lists skewness (excellent 0-0.25), orthogonal quality (good >0.7), aspect ratio (near 1:1 in the core, high but flow-aligned in boundary layers), growth rate (<=1.2), the requirement that mapped faces be 3-/4-sided with matching opposite-edge node counts, and grid independence as the overall check.

Step 3.step_name: Run the SST k-omega simulation and troubleshoot the low exit Mach number
Step 3.step_action: I ran the density-based solver with the SST k-omega model (ideal gas, Sutherland viscosity) and monitored convergence. The exit Mach number came out at ~0.40 instead of the expected ~0.51, so I described my setup and the symptom to Claude and asked for the most likely causes and fixes.

nodes.label: Configure the density-based SST k-omega solver and material properties
nodes.detail: In Fluent Setup she configures the solver as density-based and axisymmetric (since only half the model was built), enables the energy equation, and selects the SST k-omega viscous model, citing a reference Reynolds number of 5601 (turbulent) and reference temperature of 530 R (294 K) from the NASA case with a target jet Mach number of 0.51. In Materials she sets air as an ideal gas using Sutherland's law for viscosity since explicit viscosity data isn't given.

nodes.label: Define pressure-inlet/outlet boundary conditions from the NASA pressure ratio
nodes.detail: She defines pressure-inlet boundary conditions for both the 'freestream_inlet' and 'inlet' zones using a gauge total pressure computed from Pt/Pref = 1.19671 times the reference pressure 101,325 Pa (roughly 121,000-129,000 Pa depending on zone) and a temperature of 294 K, sets the inlet flow direction to axial (1,0), and configures the pressure-outlet similarly, while confirming the axis, symmetry, and no-slip wall zones were already set correctly.

nodes.label: Set up and launch the 2000-iteration solution run with Solution Steering
nodes.detail: She sets solution methods to implicit with default discretization, sets convergence criteria to none (running a fixed iteration count instead), initializes with Hybrid Initialization, and sets up 2000 iterations with Solution Steering (starting subsonic, first-order blending). She begins running, periodically pausing to manually raise the Courant number (from an initial low value up through roughly 15, 23, 45+) as residuals stabilize.

nodes.label: Ask Claude whether the residual plot indicates a converging solution
nodes.detail: Around iteration 420 she pastes a screenshot of the Scaled Residuals plot into Claude and asks 'is this solution converging?'.

nodes.label: Ask Claude to re-assess convergence after more iterations ('how about now?')
nodes.detail: After letting the run continue (residuals now shown out to iteration ~600), she pastes an updated screenshot and asks 'how about now?'. Claude answers this is 'meaningfully better' - continuity/velocity/energy have flattened around 1e-3 to 3e-3 and omega has leveled off - but flags a recurring spike around iteration 570-580 mirroring the earlier one at ~320 as a concern worth explaining before trusting the result.

nodes.label: Ask Claude to confirm the run can be stopped
nodes.detail: With residuals further flattened, she asks 'should we stop here, the solution seemed to be converged'.

nodes.label: Review the flattened residual curves once more and stop the calculation
nodes.detail: The participant checks the residual curves a final time (continuity, k, omega, velocities, and energy all flattened) and stops the run, accepting the converged solution rather than running the full 2000 iterations.

nodes.label: Response about re-assess convergence after more iterations
nodes.detail: Claude replies 'Not yet' - noting continuity/velocity/energy residuals still trending down around 1e-2 to 3e-2 with a visible spike near iteration ~320, and a sawtooth rising pattern in k and omega between iterations 50-300 that suggests the flow field is still structurally settling.

nodes.label: Response about whether the residual plot indicates a converging solution
Review Claude's response about whether the residual plot indicates a converging solution
Check the project in ANSYS Fluent

Response about confirm the run can be stopped
nodes.detail: Claude confirms: 'Yes - this looks like a genuine converged solution now, not just a lull between spikes', citing flat residuals from iteration ~800-1400 with no repeat of the earlier spikes at ~320/570.

Step 4.step_name: Analyse the jet results (contours, centreline velocity, y+ / y*)
Step 4.step_action: I extracted the Mach contours, the centreline axial-velocity and Mach profiles, and the wall y+ / y* distributions, and asked Claude to help interpret the decaying-jet behaviour (potential core, decay zone, far field) and confirm that the near-wall resolution was adequate.

nodes.label: Finish the converged run and switch to Fluent post-processing
nodes.detail: After stopping the calculation, the console shows the run reaching completion ('Calculation complete'). The participant switches from the Domain/Solution ribbon to the Results ribbon in Fluent to begin extracting flow-field results from the converged case.

nodes.label: Generate the Mach number contour and set up centerline/wall XY plots
nodes.detail: She creates a Mach Number contour (contour-1) over the nozzle/jet mesh, showing values from about 6.4e-6 up to 0.377, and opens the XY Plot dialog to define line surfaces (line-9, line-10, etc.) along the axis and wall for extracting axial velocity and Mach profiles, plotting Axial Velocity against Position for the inlet/outlet/wall-surface_body surfaces.

nodes.label: Ask Claude to explain wall y+ / y* and how to plot them to check near-wall resolution
nodes.detail: She asks Claude 'how to plot the wall y+ and y* on ansys setup and what they represent'.

nodes.label: Compare centerline velocity/Mach profiles against the NASA ASJ benchmark plots
nodes.detail: The participant opens the NASA/turbulence-model-resource-group reference webpage (tmbwg.github.io axisymmetric subsonic jet validation page) showing the benchmark 'Along Centerline' u/Ujet decay curve and cross-sectional velocity profiles at x/Djet = 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, positioning it alongside her own Fluent XY plots to visually compare her centerline velocity decay and radial profiles against the published experimental/benchmark data.

nodes.label: Response about explain wall y+ / y* and how to plot them to check near-wall resolution
nodes.detail: Claude's visible reply explains y+ = rho*u_tau*y/mu (target y+ ~ 1 for low-Re/enhanced wall treatment vs. 30-300 for wall functions) and y* = rho*C_mu^(1/4)*k_P^(1/2)*y/mu used internally by Fluent's wall functions, then walks through three ways to check it in Fluent: a Contours plot of Wall Yplus/Ystar, an XY Plot along the wall, or a Surface Integrals min/max/average report, plus the practical tip that a bad y+ means adjusting the first-layer mesh height rather than the solver.
